chunks: "A register is a small piece of storage built from flip-flops that holds a value right inside the processor.
A 32-bit register is just 32 D flip-flops sharing a clock and a write-enable.
They're the fastest memory in the system: the ALU reads its operands from registers and writes its result back to a register, usually within a single cycle, at the very top of the memory hierarchy.
A CPU has several kinds. General-purpose registers hold operands and addresses, for example RISC-V has 32 of them, 32 bits each.
Then special-purpose ones: the program counter that points at the next instruction, the stack pointer, a status register with flags like zero and carry.
Internally there are also pipeline registers between stages.
They're named directly in the instruction encoding, five bits to pick one of 32, rather than addressed like memory, which is why access is so fast and why there can only be a few.
Too many would mean bigger decoders and more ports, which slows every cycle.
And in embedded work the term also covers peripheral registers: control and status registers at fixed addresses, where individual bits enable a UART, set a baud rate or flag an interrupt.
Same idea, flip-flops with a bus interface."
